Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Diya’s delivery route had led her past a row of shuttered warehouses when a man stepped into the narrow alley, his hand tucked into his jacket as he ordered her to hand over her phone and wallet. The sudden stripping of her control, the absolute demand that she comply, still played in her mind not as a fluid sequence but as a handful of stark snapshots—the glint of his ring, the scuff of his boots, the sudden flare of her own headlights cutting the dark. Each time one of those frozen moments surfaced, the lingering threat of renewed violence seemed to surge again, sharpening her sense of danger until her muscles locked and she could not relax even in her own bed. That recurring spike of fear quickly taught her that she was fundamentally powerless, solidifying a quiet conviction that she could not stop bad things from happening to her. As that helplessness took root, Diya began to tell herself the robbery wasn’t that serious and that it did not really matter, hoping the denial would make the trauma fade, but the minimization only deepened her guilt over doing nothing to stop it. Within weeks, the memory fragments began to dictate her daily rhythms. Whenever a police cruiser rolled past her apartment or an officer’s uniform appeared on her street corner, that familiar sense of forced compliance would instantly pull those same frozen images back, bypassing her conscious thought. That sudden recall, in turn, activated a rigid habit of scanning every new space for a door or window she could bolt through, leaving her pacing her rooms instead of resting. She wakes during the night to check whether she is safe, and the constant hyper-vigilance drains her completely. Because she felt fundamentally powerless to prevent another attack, Diya turned directly to those numbing strategies, using prescription pills to shut off the mental noise. This belief that she was helpless to control her surroundings directly amplified the threat, making even ordinary street corners feel like potential ambushes. The resulting state of alertness made her hyper-sensitive to any potential threat, keeping her locked in a cycle where a suspicious glance or a sudden noise would immediately trigger the fear of being trapped again. Now, at twenty-two, Diya’s job as a delivery driver has become a daily crucible. She still maps every entrance and exit before feeling comfortable anywhere, a habit that makes her late for deliveries and leaves her supervisors confused by her erratic pacing. The avoidance of driving has shrunk her social world; she stops answering calls when her friends want to go out, certain that she is set apart from them, isolated in a way they could never understand. When she finally drove the delivery van again, the avoidance of driving and the numbing drugs had left her reactive; the sight of someone loitering near a crosswalk would instantly reignite the urge to map out a quick getaway, proving how the strategies meant to protect her were actually feeding the very cues she feared. The loop has tightened until the threat feels absolute, pushing her back toward the very strategies that keep the fear alive. She finally sought help because the substances are no longer working, because her van sits unused in the driveway, and because she is terrified she will never be able to look at the road again without feeling like she is back in that alley. What she hopes for, now, is simply to stop running from the shadows of her own mind.
